sectionsContent.title: Electronegativity & Bond Type

concept.summary: M = metal   ·   NM = nonmetal   ·   I = ionic   ·   PC = polar covalent   ·   NPC = nonpolar covalent
keyIdeas: ΔEN = higher EN − lower EN, so ΔEN is never negative.
ΔEN under 0.40 is NPC. From 0.40 to 1.80 is PC. Over 1.80 is I.

sectionsContent.directions: Element 1 is the first element written in the formula and Element 2 is the second. Mark each one M or NM. Look up both EN values in the chart at the bottom, subtract, and write ΔEN as a subtraction, like 2.96 − 2.20 = 0.76. Then use ΔEN to name the bond. Cl₂, O₂ and N₂ are elements, not compounds, so Element 1 and Element 2 are the same. Check yourself: a metal with a nonmetal should come out I, and two nonmetals should come out PC or NPC.

headers: Bond type: I, PC or NPC

keyNotes: EN values are Pauling values to two decimals (CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics). H, C, N, O, F, Na and Cl match the values already used in the course. Cutoffs follow OpenStax Chemistry 2e, the same as the U4–U5 slides.
Every ΔEN is at least 0.20 from a cutoff, so a student working from a one-decimal chart still gets the same bond type on every row.
Element 2 is NM on every row. In a binary compound the metal is written first, and two metals bond metallically (4.4), which is outside I / PC / NPC.
CO₂, CCl₄ and CF₄ have polar bonds but are nonpolar molecules because of their shape (5.4). This sheet asks about the bond only.
PH₃: H (2.20) is higher than P (2.19), so the subtraction is 2.20 − 2.19. NCl₃ catches students out: N and Cl are close (0.12), so the bond is NPC.
Left off on purpose: CH₄ (0.35) and HF (1.78) sit too close to a cutoff, and AlCl₃ (1.55) is a metal with a nonmetal but lands in the PC range.
